pos: n. (the brasen altar standing in the court of the tabernacle and temple)
etymology: Hebrew mizbeach ha-olah, altar of the ascending offering, from zabach, to slaughter in sacrifice, and alah, to go up; the altar on which the whole victim went up in smoke. Named ten times in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: The altar of burnt offering is the great brasen altar that stood in the open court, at the door of the tabernacle, and it is the first thing a worshipper met coming in. Five cubits square and three cubits high, made of shittim wood overlaid with brass, hollow, with four horns and a brasen grate, it was the place where the whole animal was consumed. “And he put the altar of burnt offering by the door of the tabernacle of the tent of the congregation, and offered upon it the burnt offering and the meat offering; as the LORD commanded Moses” (Exodus 40:29). Its position preaches the order of approach: no man came to the golden altar of incense, nor to the holy place, nor to the mercy seat, until blood had been shed in the court. The way in was through death. Hezekiah's cleansing of the house names it first among the vessels restored — “We have cleansed all the house of the LORD, and the altar of burnt offering, with all the vessels thereof, and the shewbread table, with all the vessels thereof” (2 Chronicles 29:18) — because a temple with a cold altar is no temple at all. It is distinguished in the law from the altar of sweet incense, and the blood rites of Leviticus move deliberately between the two. The brasen altar is Calvary in the court: the whole offering given, nothing reserved, the fire not going out.

Then they went in to Hezekiah the king, and said, We have cleansed all the house of the LORD, and the altar of burnt offering, with all the vessels thereof, and the shewbread table, with all the vessels thereof.
corruption_summary: The modern instinct is to move straight to intimacy with God and leave out the altar; Scripture puts the altar at the door and makes it the only way in.
corruption_paragraphs: The characteristic error is not to deny the altar but to skip it. Contemporary worship speaks fluently of encounter, presence and the Father's heart, and speaks very little of propitiation by blood, which is the thing the brasen altar existed to accomplish. The tabernacle was laid out so that this skipping was architecturally impossible: the altar stood at the door, and a man who would not stop there could not go further in. When the writer to the Hebrews explains the work of Christ he does not begin with experience but with offering and blood, and he insists that without shedding of blood there is no remission.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of approach. Access to God is not native to fallen men and is not generated by sincerity; it is purchased, and the purchase was a death. Every burnt offering wholly consumed on that brasen altar for fifteen centuries was a promissory note, and the note was paid outside Jerusalem on a Roman cross. The altar at the door is grace, not obstruction — it is God providing the way He Himself requires.

pos: n. (an idol cast from melted metal)
etymology: Hebrew massekah, a casting, from nasak, to pour out or pour forth molten metal; rendered molten image, molten god, and molten calf. Named thirteen times in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: A molten image is an idol made by pouring melted metal into a mould, and the Authorized Version distinguishes it steadily from the graven image, which is cut or carved. Both are forbidden, and the second commandment forbids them in the same breath. The first great instance is at the foot of Sinai, while the law forbidding it was still being given: “they are quickly turned aside out of the way which I commanded them; they have made them a molten image” (Deuteronomy 9:12). The law is blunt about the manufacture: “Turn ye not unto idols, nor make to yourselves molten gods: I am the LORD your God” (Leviticus 19:4). The prophets press the absurdity rather than merely the illegality. Habakkuk asks what profit there is in the thing, and then names it exactly: “What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?” (Habakkuk 2:18). The molten image is a teacher of lies, and the lie it teaches is that the maker is greater than the made and yet bows to it. Isaiah brings the whole trade to its end: those who say to the molten images, Ye are our gods, shall be turned back and greatly ashamed.

webster_full: Hebrew massekah, a casting, a molten thing.

corruption_summary: Idolatry is reduced to a quaint ancient habit about statues, when Scripture defines it by the heart's trust and makes the image a teacher of lies.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern readers are taught to treat the second commandment as spent, on the ground that nobody now melts gold into a calf. This reading mistakes the material for the sin. Habakkuk locates the evil precisely where the metal is not — in the maker of his work who trusteth therein — so that the sin is misplaced trust, and the molten image is simply trust made visible. The more serious modern error is the opposite reduction: having declared the commandment obsolete, the churches then import images into worship as teaching aids, which is exactly what the regulative principle forbids and exactly what the second commandment addresses.

The corruption to name is the historical-critical account that reads Exodus 32 as a late polemic retrojected into the wilderness period to discredit a rival northern shrine. The text presents itself as narrative of events at Sinai, Moses records it against his own brother and his own nation, and the New Testament treats it as history and as warning. A people who had just heard the voice out of the fire cast a calf out of their earrings within forty days. That is not a literary device. That is what the human heart does with glory, and it is why the commandment stands.

pos: n. (one of the storied chambers built against the wall of the temple)
etymology: Hebrew tsela, a rib, a side, and thence a side chamber; the chambers were ribs along the flank of the house. Named in the Authorized Version in Ezekiel's temple vision.
biblical_def: The side chambers were small rooms built in three storeys against the outer wall of the house of the LORD, running round it on every side except the front. Solomon built them: “And against the wall of the house he built chambers round about, against the walls of the house round about, both of the temple and of the oracle: and he made chambers round about” (1 Kings 6:5). Ezekiel measures them in his vision of the restored house: “After he measured the wall of the house, six cubits; and the breadth of every side chamber, four cubits, round about the house on every side” (Ezekiel 41:5), and then notes their arrangement, three one over another and thirty in order. The construction detail carries the point. The beams of the chambers rested on ledges cut into the temple wall, which narrowed as it rose, so that the chambers leaned on the house without being let into it: “that they might have hold, but they had not hold in the wall of the house” (Ezekiel 41:6). Nothing pierced the sanctuary. The chambers served for storing tithes, vessels, and the priests' portions, and for the priests' use when they came off duty. They are the ordinary offices of the house, leaning on the holy place and never intruding into it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Side chamber, one of the small rooms built in three stories against the outer wall of the temple, resting on ledges in the wall but not let into it, used for stores and for the priests.

corruption_summary: Scripture's building measurements are dismissed as tedious filler; the construction of the side chambers is itself a doctrine of reverence.
corruption_paragraphs: The common treatment of these chapters is to skip them. Ezekiel 40 through 42 and 1 Kings 6 are counted among the dull places of the Bible, useful to architects and nobody else, and the reader who skips them loses a lesson the Holy Ghost thought worth cubits and courses to teach. The chambers lean on the house; they do not breach it. Everything useful, administrative and ordinary in the service of God was arranged so that it touched the sanctuary without penetrating it. That is a working definition of reverence, and it was built in stone before it was ever stated in a proposition.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God gives the pattern of His own worship down to the ledges in a wall. The regulative principle is not a Puritan invention imposed on a silent Bible; it is the plain inference from a God who measured the side chambers. Where Scripture has spoken about His house, men are not free to improve on it, and where it has not spoken, they are not free to add.

pos: n. (the vestibule at the east front of the temple)
etymology: Hebrew ulam, a porch or vestibule, from a root meaning to be in front; the forepart of the house. The phrase occurs once in the Authorized Version, 1 Kings 7:21.
biblical_def: The porch was the vestibule across the east front of the temple, twenty cubits broad and ten cubits deep: “And the porch before the temple of the house, twenty cubits was the length thereof, according to the breadth of the house; and ten cubits was the breadth thereof before the house” (1 Kings 6:3). It is where the two great pillars stood: “And he set up the pillars in the porch of the temple” (1 Kings 7:21). The porch is the threshold of the house, and Scripture uses it as the place where the state of Israel's religion is read off. When Hezekiah describes the apostasy he inherited, he names the porch first: “Also they have shut up the doors of the porch, and put out the lamps, and have not burned incense nor offered burnt offerings in the holy place unto the God of Israel” (2 Chronicles 29:7). Shut doors in the porch meant a dead house. Joel sets the priests weeping between the porch and the altar, and it is in exactly that place that Ezekiel is shown five and twenty men with their backs toward the temple of the LORD, worshipping the sun toward the east. The porch is where men turn — in or out, toward the house or away from it — and the two directions in Ezekiel 8 and Joel 2 are the whole history of Judah in a few cubits of pavement.

corruption_summary: A church's threshold is treated as a matter of hospitality and welcome; Scripture treats the porch as the place where a people's religion is declared either living or shut up.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary church-growth literature gives great attention to the entrance — the welcome, the first seven minutes, the removal of barriers — and almost none to what the entrance is an entrance to. Scripture is interested in the porch for the opposite reason. The doors of the porch stood shut under Ahaz, the lamps were out, the incense unburned; the problem was not unwelcoming architecture but a house no longer in use. Hezekiah's reformation did not redesign the porch. He opened the doors, lit the lamps, and restored the offerings.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that access and worship are not the same thing, and that the first cannot substitute for the second. Ezekiel's five and twenty men were inside the gate, standing in the right place, facing the wrong way. It is possible to gather a congregation into the porch of the house with their backs to it. What the porch exists for is the altar and the holy place beyond it, and a threshold that leads nowhere is the saddest thing in the building.

pos: n. (the court nearest the house, the court of the priests)
etymology: Hebrew chatser ha-penimith, the inner court, from chatser, an enclosure or court, and panim, the face or inward part. Named nineteen times in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: The inner court is the enclosure nearest the house of the LORD, divided from the outer court and reserved for the service of the altar. Solomon built it of hewn stone and cedar: “And he built the inner court with three rows of hewed stone, and a row of cedar beams” (1 Kings 6:36). It is where the brasen altar stood, and where the priests and Levites ministered; Ezekiel's vision measures its gates and its chambers in detail. The phrase also carries into the courts of kings, where the inner court was the place a man entered only when called — Esther risked her life to come in uncalled. Scripture uses the distinction between the courts to teach degrees of nearness. Israel came into the outer court; the priests served in the inner; the high priest alone passed within the veil, and that once a year with blood. The gradation was not snobbery but instruction: God is approachable, and He is approachable on His terms. The most terrible scene in Ezekiel happens here — “And he brought me into the inner court of the LORD'S house” (Ezekiel 8:16), and there in the holiest ground short of the sanctuary itself, five and twenty men had turned their backs on the temple to worship the rising sun. Nearness of place is not nearness of heart.

corruption_summary: Degrees of nearness to God are read as mere clericalism; Scripture uses the courts to teach that access is real and is on God's terms.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors meet at the inner court. The first is sacerdotal: the Roman and Anglo-Catholic reading takes the gradation of courts as permanent, and builds a priesthood that stands between the people and God in the new covenant as the sons of Aaron did in the old. The epistle to the Hebrews is written against precisely this, and the rent veil answers it. The second error is the modern evangelical flattening, which treats all distinctions of holiness as pretension, and so loses the fear of God along with the fences.

The dictionary holds the Reformed and Baptist position: the courts were real and the gradation was God's, and it has been fulfilled, not abolished by sentiment. Every believer is now a priest with access into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, which is a greater nearness than the inner court ever gave to any Levite. But Ezekiel 8 stands as the warning that attends it. Those men were standing in the inner court, as near as a layman could get, with their backs to the house. Privilege of position is not piety, and it never was.

pos: n. (the two brasen pillars set in the porch of Solomon's temple)
etymology: Hebrew Yakin, he shall establish, from kun, to establish or set firm; and Boaz, understood in the Authorized Version's margin as in it is strength, from az, strength. Named together in 1 Kings 7:21 and 2 Chronicles 3:17.
biblical_def: Jachin and Boaz were the two great pillars of cast brass, eighteen cubits high, that Hiram made and Solomon set up in the porch of the temple: “And he set up the pillars in the porch of the temple: and he set up the right pillar, and called the name thereof Jachin: and he set up the left pillar, and called the name thereof Boaz” (1 Kings 7:21). Each was crowned with a chapiter of five cubits, wrought with network, wreathen work, lily work and pomegranates. They bore no roof; they carried nothing. Their whole office was to be named. The names are a sentence: Jachin, he shall establish; Boaz, in it is strength. Set at the entrance of the house, they preached to everyone who came in that the establishing and the strength were not Israel's and not Solomon's, but the LORD's, and that the house stood because He upheld it. The Chaldeans broke them in pieces and carried the brass to Babylon, which proved the inscription rather than refuting it: the pillars never were the strength, and the kingdom whose temple fell was restored because He who establishes had said so. Zerubbabel laid a second foundation, and the promise ran forward to a greater house. Christ is the one who establishes, and the pillar in the temple of God is, in the end, a man He has overcome for.

corruption_summary: The pillars have been annexed by freemasonry as emblems of a secret order; in Scripture they are a public sermon that God alone establishes His house.
corruption_paragraphs: The clearest corruption of Jachin and Boaz is their appropriation by speculative freemasonry, where the two pillars became furniture of the lodge and carriers of an esoteric meaning disclosed by degrees to initiates. This inverts their biblical function exactly. The pillars stood in the porch, at the public entrance, where every worshipper passed between them, and their names were not a secret to be earned but a confession to be read. A thing God set in the open to declare His own strength has been taken indoors to flatter men with hidden knowledge.

The second corruption is the reading that treats them as mere Phoenician ornament, borrowed from Tyrian temple design by way of Hiram, and so empty of revelation. Hiram's craftsmanship is in the text and so is the naming, and it is Scripture, not the historian, that records what the names mean. The dictionary takes the naming as the point. Two pillars that held up nothing were given names that say the LORD holds up everything, and then they were broken and carried to Babylon, and He established the house anyway.

pos: n. (the great brasen laver of Solomon's temple)
etymology: Hebrew yam mutsaq, a cast or molten sea, from yam, a sea, and yatsaq, to pour out or cast metal; called also the brasen sea and the sea of brass. Named as the molten sea twice.
biblical_def: The molten sea was the enormous cast-brass basin that stood in the court of Solomon's temple, holding the water for the priests' washing: “And he made a molten sea, ten cubits from the one brim to the other: it was round all about, and his height was five cubits: and a line of thirty cubits did compass it round about” (1 Kings 7:23). It rested on twelve brasen oxen, three facing each quarter, and was ornamented beneath the brim with knops and lily work. It is called a sea because of its size; the tabernacle's laver had been a vessel a man could carry, and this held, by the account in Kings, two thousand baths. The thing it supplied was washing. Blood was dealt with at the altar; water was dealt with here, and no priest went into the holy place with unwashed hands and feet. The two together give the whole of the believer's standing — the altar for guilt and the sea for defilement, justification and sanctification in brass and water, and neither one optional for a man who meant to serve. The Chaldeans broke it up: “the brasen sea that was in the house of the LORD, did the Chaldees break in pieces, and carried the brass of them to Babylon” (2 Kings 25:13). In the Revelation the sea before the throne is no longer for washing but is of glass, clear as crystal, because in that house the washing is finished.

corruption_summary: The sanctuary's washing is collapsed into its sacrifice, as though cleansing were nothing once guilt is answered; Scripture sets the altar and the sea in the same court.
corruption_paragraphs: The antinomian error treats the altar as having made the sea unnecessary — guilt answered, therefore defilement indifferent, and holiness an optional refinement for the earnest. The architecture of the court refutes it. Both stood there, and the priest who passed the altar and skipped the sea did not enter the holy place. Justification and sanctification are distinct and inseparable: the first is a verdict and the second a work, and the same Christ who is the propitiation is also the one who washes His church with water by the word.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the washing is for those already belonging to the house. Only priests used the sea; it was not for the nations outside but for men already consecrated, who yet got dirty doing holy work. That is the Christian life. The sea of glass in Revelation 4 is the end of it, standing clear and still before the throne because there is nothing left to wash off, and the twelve oxen that bore the water have become a multitude that no man can number.

pos: n. (the lily-shaped ornament wrought on the chapiters of the temple pillars)
etymology: Hebrew maaseh shushan, work of the lily, from shushan, a lily, and maaseh, work or workmanship. Named twice in the Authorized Version, both of Solomon's pillars.
biblical_def: Lily work is the ornament wrought upon the chapiters that crowned the two brasen pillars of Solomon's temple: “And the chapiters that were upon the top of the pillars were of lily work in the porch, four cubits” (1 Kings 7:19). The record of the pillars closes with it: “And upon the top of the pillars was lily work: so was the work of the pillars finished” (1 Kings 7:22). The brim of the molten sea was wrought in the same spirit, like the brim of a cup, with flowers of lilies. The lily is the flower the Song of Solomon gives to the beloved and the flower our Lord sets against Solomon's own glory, telling His disciples to consider how the lilies grow, and that Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of them. There is a quiet irony in it: Solomon crowned his pillars with brass lilies, and the Lord pointed to a real one in a field and said it was better dressed. The lily work is the last thing named in the making of the pillars, the finishing touch on the strongest objects in the court. Eighteen cubits of cast brass, and the thing that completed them was a flower. God's house was not merely strong; it was beautiful, and the beauty was commanded as the strength was.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Lily work, the lily-shaped ornament wrought upon the chapiters of the two pillars in the porch of Solomon's temple, with which the work of the pillars was finished.
webster_full: Hebrew maaseh shushan, work of the lily.

Wrought upon the chapiters of the pillars, four cubits, 1 Kings 7:19.
The last thing named in the finishing of the pillars, 1 Kings 7:22.
The brim of the molten sea was wrought with flowers of lilies, 1 Kings 7:26.
scriptures: And the chapiters that were upon the top of the pillars were of lily work in the porch, four cubits.

Mat 6:28
And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:
corruption_summary: Beauty in the house of God is treated as either worldliness or as the point itself; Scripture makes it commanded workmanship, subordinate to the worship it adorns.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors attend ornament in worship. The bare utilitarian instinct, common among heirs of the Reformation who have forgotten what the Reformation actually said, treats all beauty in the house of God as suspect, as though plainness were a virtue in itself. Solomon's pillars answer it: God specified lily work. The opposite error, far better funded, makes the building and its aesthetic the substance of the religion, so that the congregation is moved by architecture and lighting rather than by the Word preached and the ordinances kept.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that beauty in God's house is a servant and not a master. The lily work finished the pillars; it did not hold them up. It was commanded, which settles the question of whether it is permissible, and it was ornamental, which settles the question of whether it is central. A church may be beautiful and must be faithful, and when the lilies of the field outdress Solomon it is because the Maker of both is better at glory than we are.

pos: n. (chain-work of twisted gold on the high priest's breastplate)
etymology: From the archaic English wreathen, the old past participle of wreathe, to twist or plait; rendering Hebrew migbaloth, twisted or plaited work, from gabal, to twist together. Named four times in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Wreathen work is twisted or plaited chain-work of pure gold, commanded for the fastening of the high priest's breastplate to the ephod: “And two chains of pure gold at the ends; of wreathen work shalt thou make them, and fasten the wreathen chains to the ouches” (Exodus 28:14). The command is repeated for the breastplate itself — “And thou shalt make upon the breastplate chains at the ends of wreathen work of pure gold” (Exodus 28:22) — and the execution is recorded in the same words in Exodus 39. Wreathen is the older English past participle of wreathe, to twist, and has since been displaced by wreathed; the Authorized Version keeps the strong form. The function is the doctrine. These chains held the breastplate of judgment, bearing the twelve stones graven with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, upon Aaron's heart whenever he went in before the LORD. The plaited gold was what kept the names from falling. Aaron did not carry Israel into the holy place in his hand, where he might set them down, nor in his memory, where he might forget them; they were chained to his heart with twisted gold. Our great High Priest needs no chains, and the names He bears in before the Father cannot be lost.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Wreathen work, twisted or plaited chain-work of pure gold, by which the breastplate of judgment was fastened to the ouches of the ephod; wreathen being the older past participle of wreathe.
webster_full: Archaic English wreathen, the old past participle of wreathe, to twist or plait.
Since displaced in common use by wreathed; the Authorized Version keeps the strong form.

scriptures: And two chains of pure gold at the ends; of wreathen work shalt thou make them, and fasten the wreathen chains to the ouches.
And thou shalt make upon the breastplate chains at the ends of wreathen work of pure gold.

And they put the two wreathen chains of gold in the two rings on the ends of the breastplate.
corruption_summary: An archaic participle makes a plain verse look obscure, and the doctrine it carries — the names of the tribes chained over the priest's heart — is passed over.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is linguistic before it is doctrinal. Wreathen is a strong past participle of the kind English has been steadily losing, and a reader who does not recognise it reads past the verse rather than through it, taking the phrase for untranslatable ritual detail. The result is that one of the richest pictures of priestly intercession in the Pentateuch is skipped because of a vowel. The dictionary exists for exactly this: the word means twisted, the chains were plaited gold, and the verse is about what held the names of Israel over Aaron's heart.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the security of those the High Priest represents. Aaron's breastplate was fastened with gold chains because the names upon it were not to be set down or shaken loose, and the whole apparatus of ouches and wreathen work exists to say so in metal. Christ bears His people in before the Father by a better covenant and an unchangeable priesthood, and none of them is lost. The chains were a picture of a thing that no longer needs chains.
